articles.title: Towards scalable cancer prognosis by aligning semi-supervised learning with survival modeling.
articles.abstract: Prognostic assessment via whole-slide images (WSIs) is a key task in computational pathology. However, the development of robust predictive models is often bottlenecked by the scarcity of survival-annotated data, given the longitudinal nature of clinical follow-up. Despite its potential, semi-supervised learning (SSL) remains underexplored in this field. Existing SSL methods, primarily designed for natural image classification, rely on the assumption of marginally independent categories, which makes them difficult to adapt to the high-dimensional complexity of WSIs and the temporal continuity inherent in survival outcomes. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel semi-supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) framework tailored for WSI-based prognosis. Specifically, we first introduce a morphology-perceived MIL network (Morph-MIL) that jointly models tissue composition and global semantic representations. To maintain a stable reference, a dynamic memory bank is employed to encapsulate the multi-level representations of labeled samples (censored & uncensored). Furthermore, we develop a pseudo-labeling strategy that assigns discrete labels containing temporal relationships to annotation-free data by aligning their features with the memory bank through bin-wise aggregation. Comprehensive evaluation establishes the superiority of the proposed framework, while extensive ablation analyses and visualizations confirm its efficacy in prognostic prediction and biological interpretation. Consequently, this study offers a scalable solution for WSI survival modeling in scenarios with limited annotations. The code is available at: https://github.com/yihuangswust-alt/SSL-Morph_MIL.

articles.title: PSGMM++: Pulmonary Segment Segmentation with Anatomical Insights.
articles.abstract: The lung has a complex hierarchical structure comprising lobes and pulmonary segments. Pulmonary segments are not segmented based on visual features, but rather on anatomical knowledge that each segment is centered on a bronchus or artery, far from the intersegmental borders. In this paper, we propose PSGMM++, an extension of PSGMM, for pulmonary segment segmentation with anatomical insights. PSGMM leverages spatial information of bronchial and vascular structures and generates probability maps using Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) for each pulmonary segment's location, addressing the limitation of existing image-based segmentation models that lack the understanding of positional priors. Building upon PSGMM, PSGMM++ further enhances segmentation performance by explicitly incorporating anatomical relationships and utilizing local geometric features effectively. The centroids of each GMM component are located on the bronchus or artery, ensuring that the intersegmental borders are positioned away from these central structures. The covariance and weight are defined by local features extracted around each centroid, making them sensitive to local structural variations. As the training approach shifts from voxel-wise classification to classwise probability distribution generation, we introduce a novel loss function designed to maximize likelihood while satisfying the constraint of each GMM parameter through the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, named EM loss. Built on a solid theoretical foundation, it provides explainability when applied to pre-surgical navigation. Furthermore, PSGMM++ demonstrates effective and flexible performance due to its efficient design.

articles.title: Zero Echo Time Functional MRI in Humans: Technical Demonstration and Proof-of-Concept.
articles.abstract: Conventional EPI-based fMRI relies on the BOLD contrast to map activity changes, but is limited by high acoustic noise, susceptibility artifacts, and distortion near air-tissue interfaces. Ultra-short and zero-echo-time (ZTE) sequences have gained considerable attention in animal fMRI studies due to their robustness against susceptibility effects, low acoustic noise, and ability to capture signal sources distinct from those of conventional BOLD imaging. In this study, we present a feasibility-level proof-of-concept technical demonstration of ZTE-based fMRI in humans at 3T, while maintaining many of the advantages observed in preclinical studies. Phantom measurements demonstrate that the ZTE protocol is sensitive to oxygenation-related T1 changes at 3T, supporting its feasibility for detecting related functional signals. In five healthy volunteers, task-based visual stimulation and finger tapping experiments elicited activation in primary visual and motor cortices, respectively, using the ZTE sequence, demonstrating proof-of-concept feasibility in this small cohort. Resting-state components with spatial patterns consistent with canonical visual and sensorimotor networks were identified using independent component analysis in the same cohort. Compared to BOLD-EPI, ZTE showed significantly reduced acoustic noise and was largely insensitive to susceptibility-induced signal loss in this feasibility study. While this work represents our initial experience using ZTE for human fMRI at 3T, the presented results will motivate future studies to refine and extend this approach to explore complementary functional contrast mechanisms.

articles.title: ZonoSeg: A Zonal-aware Prostate Segmentation Framework on 3D MRI images.
articles.abstract: Accurate zonal-aware prostate segmentation in clinical 3D MRI is important for diagnosis and treatment planning. However, delineating the central-gland-peripheral-zone interface remains challenging because gradual tissue transitions, irregular internal boundaries, and pathology-induced appearance variations can lead to clinically relevant zonal boundary errors. We propose ZonoSeg, a hierarchical encoder-decoder framework that targets these ambiguous boundaries via uncertainty-aware, boundary-sensitive feature transmission in stage-wise skip connections. The ZonoSeg Block combines edge cues with learnable multi-scale Gaussian smoothing to construct a continuous probabilistic boundary field, and the ZAD head further refines zonal separation through explicit foreground-background interactions. Experiments demonstrate improved boundary localization and robust zonal segmentation on both dual-target and single-target tasks across eight multi-center prostate MRI datasets; on PROMISE MRI BMC, ZonoSeg achieves Dice scores of 83.39% for the central gland and 84.10% for the peripheral zone, with HD95 of 3.84 mm and 3.41 mm, respectively. Code: https://github.com/deepang-ai/ZonoSeg.

articles.title: Improved Visualization of Heart Valves With 4D-CT Using a Novel Motion Correction Algorithm.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Motion artifacts remain a limitation of cardiac CT when assessing both native and prosthetic heart valves, particularly during phases of rapid motion. This may lead to reduced image quality, potentially impairing the evaluation of valvular movement and pathology. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether a novel reconstruction-based motion correction algorithm improves image quality and reduces motion artifacts of native and prosthetic heart valves compared with standard reconstructions in photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT). MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective single-center study, 57 patients [21 women; median age, 71 (interquartile range, 57 to 78 y)] who underwent clinically indicated 4D cardiac CT for suspected native and prosthetic valvular disease were included. Images were acquired using retrospectively electrocardiography (ECG)-gated spiral dual-source PCD-CT without ECG-pulsing. Images were reconstructed in 10% steps throughout the RR-interval using both standard (TrueStack) and an otherwise identical reconstruction using the novel motion correction algorithm (ZeeFreePlus). Subjective image quality and motion artifacts were independently assessed by 2 blinded, experienced readers using a 4-point visual analog scale for 3 categories: valve frame/annulus, valve leaflets, and valvular pathology. Objective analysis included quantification of the volume of artifacts throughout the cardiac cycle. RESULTS: A total of 68 valves were evaluated, including 57 prosthetic valves (22 transcatheter aortic valve replacements and 19 surgical valves, 11 mitral valves, and 5 tricuspid valve interventions) and 11 native valves. Valvular pathology was present in 29 cases, with the most prevalent being hypoattenuated leaflet thickening in 14/29 (48%). Motion-corrected reconstructions significantly improved image quality and reduced motion artifacts across all cardiac phases and all categories (all, P<0.001). The largest improvements were observed during systole, particularly at 10% of the RR-interval, with significantly greater gains than during diastole (P<0.05). Improvements were consistent across aortic and atrioventricular prosthetic valves and translated into improved visualization of valvular pathology (P<0.001). Objective quantitative analysis corroborated the subjective image quality findings by demonstrating reductions in the volumes of motion-induced artifacts when using the algorithm (P<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: A novel motion correction algorithm substantially reduced motion artifacts and improved image quality in both native and prosthetic heart valve imaging with PCD-CT, with the largest improvements in systole. These benefits resulted in enhanced visualization of valvular pathology, potentially reinforcing the growing clinical role of cardiac CT for the assessment of valve disease.

articles.title: Colour maps for representation of quantitative metrics in radiology: meaningful or misleading?
articles.abstract: The increased utility of quantitative metrics in medical imaging has prompted the use of colour representation of the data. Colour schemes for image display can highlight pathology and distinguish normal anatomy, thus potentially aiding image interpretation. Adding colour schemes to images may serve the sole purpose of visualising an abnormality or may seek to represent and meaningfully convey a quantitative metric. An early use of colour representation is exemplified by colour Doppler in ultrasound (US), where a two-sided linear scale is commonly applied. More recently, many schemes have arisen, ranging from a single colour to depict a segmented region to a range of colours that embrace the entire colour spectrum. These may be applied as continuous or discrete palettes, depending on the software vendor or even on individual user settings. The lack of standardisation of colour schemes across the medical community, especially in medical imaging, risks misinterpretation of quantitative data and potential unintended negative clinical consequences. The purpose of this article is to review the colour schemes used for quantitative imaging across US, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography (PET), the way in which they are applied, the clinical applications where their use is desirable for enhanced interpretation, and the pitfalls where standardisation is lacking in a variety of clinical applications. Finally, we discuss some solutions that could be employed to enable standardisation and augment the use of colour in image interpretation. KEY POINTS: Question Colour schemes in medical imaging can highlight pathology, but standardisation is lacking for most imaging modalities, thus risking misinterpretation of quantitative data. Findings For T1, T2, and T2* maps and their inverses, colour map recommendations have recently been proposed, but are mostly lacking for other quantitative data. Critical relevance statement Standardised colour maps can enhance data analyses across scanners and institutions, which is important for multicentre studies and handling big data. Furthermore, standardised and harmonised colour maps could improve lesion conspicuity, cross-platform comparability, and longitudinal reliability.

articles.title: Adult diagnostic reference levels in computed tomography: A systematic review and analysis of regional variability.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Computed tomography (CT) is vital in diagnostic imaging but involves ionizing radiation, requiring careful dose management. Diagnostic Reference Levels (DRLs), recommended by the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP), serve as benchmarks for optimizing radiation doses and improving patient safety. While many DRL studies exist, most focus on individual countries, anatomical regions, or clinical indications, limiting broader applicability. This systematic review addresses this gap by analyzing adult CT DRLs across continents and major anatomical areas. It compares international benchmarks, highlights methodological inconsistencies, and explores drivers of regional variability to inform global dose optimization. METHODS: Following PRISMA-S guidelines, a systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase identified studies published in English from 2018 to 2025. Keywords related to DRLs and CT imaging were used. Studies reporting DRLs for adult CT using standardized dose metrics were included. Pediatric studies, narrative reviews, Phantom studies, case reports, pilot studies, and gray literature were excluded. RESULTS: Of 2719 identified articles, 63 met the inclusion criteria. Local DRLs were reported in 48 % of studies, and national DRLs in 52 %. Substantial variability was observed across examination types and geographical regions. For head CT, CTDIvol values ranged from 38.2 to 117.6 mGy, while DLP values ranged from 512 to 1943 mGy·cm across the included studies. Similar variability was observed for other examination categories, which may reflect differences in patient characteristics, equipment, and imaging protocols. CONCLUSION: This systematic review identified substantial international variability in DRLs for adult CT examinations, associated with differences in imaging practices, patient characteristics, available technology, and methodological approaches to DRL establishment. The 75th percentile was the most commonly used method for defining DRLs across the included studies. These findings support regular DRL review and greater methodological standardization to improve comparability across regions and strengthen CT dose optimization practices.

articles.title: Ultrasound-guided injection treatments for tendinopathy: an update.
articles.abstract: The choice of treatment for chronic tendinopathy and related peritendinous conditions has become challenging as multiple options are available. When conservative treatments fail, injections of platelet-rich plasma (PRP), corticosteroids, and hyaluronic acid have become important in the management of these conditions. Other interventions, such as dry-needling, percutaneous tenotomy, percutaneous release, and hydrodissection, may also be used. Ultrasound guidance allows real-time visualization of the needle relative to its target and adjacent neurovascular structures. This is particularly advantageous for deep or small-caliber tendons, for procedures requiring precise intratendinous or peritendinous needle placement (e.g., PRP injection, hydrodissection), and for percutaneous release, where a blind approach carries a materially higher risk of neurovascular or tendon injury. This review summarizes the mechanism of action, technique, evidence, and indications for the injection treatments currently used for tendinopathy, and outlines the general principles of ultrasound-guided injection technique.

Acute glenoid rim fractures: reliability of linear and surface area methods for CT-based bone loss assessment.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: We wanted to investigate and compare the reliability of two measuring methods for glenoid bone loss, one linear- and one surface area method, in acute glenoid fractures after dislocation. This was an experimental study. METHOD: Thirty CT-shoulder scans in patients with an acute glenoid rim fracture were measured in a lateral"en face" view in 2D and 3D by two independent assessors. In 10 of 30 patients contralateral shoulder CT-scan was obtained for reference circle placement. Intra- and interrater reliability was analysed by Intra Class Correlation. Wilcoxon signed rank test was performed for comparison of bone loss estimates between methods. RESULTS: The reliability ranged from 0.85 to 0.97 for the two methods in both 2D and 3D, which is considered good to excellent. The bone loss estimates were significantly larger with linear method than area method. Drawing of a best-fitting-circle had a good reliability between assessors. CONCLUSIONS: Linear- and surface area methods demonstrated comparable reliability in assessing glenoid bone loss in acute fractures and we found no difference between 2D- and 3D-modalities. However, linear methods may overestimate defect in cases with irregular fracture lines, suggesting area method may be preferable in acute fractures.

articles.title: Implementation of a Structured Peer Learning Program and Missed Critical Findings in a Large Integrated Radiology Practice: A Baseline Retrospective Analysis.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: The American College of Radiology (ACR) defines peer learning as nonpunitive, education-centered case review, separated from individual performance evaluation. We describe a program designed against ACR criteria in a large integrated practice and report first-cycle metrics, including missed critical findings-a narrow subset of major misses. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective analysis spanned 283 radiologists across more than 100 sites between March 30 and May 14, 2026. Cases entered through voluntary worklist submission, risk-event referral, and departmental escalation, and were adjudicated by a fellowship-trained coordinator. A missed critical finding (MCF) required both a finding on the institutional critical results list (provider notification within 30 minutes) and a 4B classification, with agreement between two independent reviewers. Exact (Poisson) 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. RESULTS: Of 702 submissions, 489 (69.7%) were Learning Opportunities, 187 (26.6%) Great Calls, and 26 (3.7%) Agrees. Of 283 radiologists, 182 (64.3%) submitted at least one case, and 213 (75.3%) received feedback; two conferences were held. Of 17 candidates, reviewers concurred on 7 at initial review; the 10 discordant were resolved by consensus, none meeting criteria. Across 409,122 interpreted studies, the confirmed MCF rate was 0.017 per 1000 (95% CI 0.007-0.035). Seven radiologists (2.5%) had one event; none had more. No confirmed event had been independently filed as a safety event. CONCLUSION: The MCF rate reflects a narrow, time-critical subset ascertained with unmeasured sensitivity against a diluted denominator. It is a conservative internal baseline, not a measure of diagnostic accuracy or individual performance.

articles.title: Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the feasibility of a quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-to-structured reporting pipeline that integrates quantitative MRI software with large language models (LLMs) for structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers and generating clinician-facing report conclusions. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A total of 192 patients with 3D T1 and 2D or 3D FLAIR MRI images from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative database were randomly selected. A deep-learning model generated structured report findings based on nine indices related to brain atrophy, white matter hyperintensities, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) space abnormalities, and compared with neuroradiologist-generated reference reports. Four LLMs (GPT-OSS 20B, MedGemma 4B, Phi-3, and Llama 3.1 8B) generated clinician-facing conclusions from the structured findings. Generated conclusions were evaluated using a five-point Likert scale across four metrics (accuracy, relevance, clarity, and satisfaction). Output errors were assessed across four categories: language, omission, addition, and numeric errors. RESULTS: Structured report findings demonstrated high accuracy for CSF space analysis (77.6%-97.9%). Performance for ordinal visual scales was lower under strict matching (27.1%-57.8%) but improved with a one-grade tolerance (91.7%-97.4%). Among LLMs, GPT achieved the highest scores across most metrics (median score 5) and exhibited the lowest output error rates. Smaller models (Phi-3 and Llama 3.1 8B) showed overall lower performance, with more language, omission, and addition errors. MedGemma demonstrated intermediate performance, but the highest rate of numeric errors. CONCLUSION: Our quantitative MRI-to-structured reporting pipeline, integrating quantitative MRI software with LLM-based conclusion generation, might be feasible for automated structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers.

articles.title: Evaluating Perfusion Quantification for Phase-Resolved Functional Lung MRI Using Gaussian Filtering.
articles.abstract: Phase-resolved functional lung (PREFUL) MRI enables contrast-free lung perfusion quantification (QQuant). Current quantification uses a single median value per slice of maximal blood exchange fraction (ΔS), which limits regional assessment, whereas regional ΔS causes artifacts. This retrospective study aims to optimize QQuant by applying Gaussian filtering to ΔS to improve intrascan/interscan repeatability in healthy volunteers, while evaluating whether the optimized QQuant retains agreement with dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) patients and exhibits a physiologically plausible gravity-dependent perfusion gradient. Analysis was performed on 29 healthy subjects (11 female, age: 19-33 years), 20 COPD patients (three female, age: 46-76 years) and 15 CTEPH patients (six female, age: 44-82 years), scanned at 1.5 T. Healthy subjects underwent four PREFUL scans in two sessions. Patients just underwent one PREFUL and DCE scan. QQuant maps were calculated while applying different Gaussian filter options to ΔS. In patients, PREFUL-derived QQuant maps were coregistered to DCE-derived pulmonary blood flow (PBF) maps for global and voxel-wise correlations. In healthy subjects, the gravity-dependent perfusion gradient was quantified by linear regression of slice-wise QQuant across five coronal slices. Gaussian filtering ΔS with σ = 1.5 improved intrascan and interscan repeatability in healthy subjects (mean bias: ≤ 2.94 mL/100 mL; Cohen's d: 0.2) compared with the current slice median setting (mean bias: ≥ 3.75 mL/100 mL; Cohen's d: 0.68). Correlations with PBF remained stable after filtering (σ = 1.5) in COPD (filtered vs. default ΔS: global r = 0.57 vs. r = 0.59, voxel-wise r = 0.32 vs. r = 0.32) and CTEPH (global r = 0.32 vs. r = 0.28, voxel-wise r = 0.40 vs. r = 0.41), all significant except global CTEPH. The filtered QQuant maps showed a significant gravity-dependent perfusion gradient (ΔS filtered σ = 1.5) of 1.47 mL/min/100 mL/cm. Gaussian filtering ΔS with σ = 1.5 improved QQuant repeatability while preserving DCE-MRI agreement and is therefore recommended. The observed gravity-dependent perfusion gradient confirms physiological plausibility, supporting potential in clinical use.

articles.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Inguinal Node Relapse Risk in Anal Squamous Cell Carcinoma Following Chemoradiotherapy Omitting Prophylactic Inguinal Node Irradiation.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Prophylactic inguinal node irradiation (PINI) is standard in chemoradiotherapy for anal squamous cell carcinoma. However, PINI increases toxicity, including bowel and sexual dysfunction, bone marrow suppression, and lymphoedema. Evidence on inguinal node relapse risk without PINI remains limited, warranting systematic review. METHODS: A systematic literature review was performed in accordance with the PRISMA standards using using Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library and Pubmed for relevant studies between 1980 and 2025. Studies of > 10 patients treated with chemoradiotherapy without PINI and a minimum FU of 24 months were included. Data on stage, recurrence, staging investigations, and radiotherapy technique was extracted and analysed. RESULTS: Nine papers were identified satisfying predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, included 727 patients. All 9 reported individual outcomes for stages grouped as T1/2 and T3/4, 6 papers detailed outcomes for individual stages. The pooled estimated risk of lymph node relapse in T1/2 patients is 8.0% (95% CI 6.0-10.6). The pooled analysis for T1 and T2 tumours respectively were 2.20% (95% CI 0.5-8.3) and 8.7 (95% CI 5.4-13.7). CONCLUSIONS: The quantification of inguinal relapse rates supports existing clinical practise that in selected patients, with T1 tumours or the frail and co-morbid population, it may be appropriate to omit PINI. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: Following the recently published ACT4 study, suggesting that reduction of dose does not reduce morbidity, this research suggests that exclusion of inguinal nodes in early-stage tumours may be an alternative strategy and should be investigated further in clinical trials.

articles.title: Prandial Effects on Intravoxel Incoherent Motion Quantification in the Liver.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the feasibility of detecting prandial (i.e., meal) induced changes in microvascular flow in the liver, including changes in the spatial distribution of flow velocities, using intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) MRI. METHODS: Thirteen (n = 13) healthy volunteers underwent two liver MR exams: one preprandial after fasting and one postprandial after ingesting nutrition shakes. IVIM data were acquired four times: twice preprandial to evaluate repeatability using coefficients of variation (CV) and twice postprandial to evaluate meal-induced changes relative to preprandial estimates. 4D flow MRI was acquired once pre- and postprandial to estimate portal venous flow rate, which was normalized by liver volume to evaluate correlations with IVIM. IVIM estimates of the diffusion coefficient (D), R2-corrected perfusion signal fraction (Fc), blood velocity standard deviation (Vb), and spatial volumes associated with slow microvascular flow (Ω1), fast microvascular flow (Ω2), and major vessels (Ω3) were determined. RESULTS: Significantly (p ≤ 0.01) higher Vb and Ω2 volume and lower Ω1 volume were observed postprandial compared to preprandial. The magnitudes of the postprandial changes in Vb, Ω1 volume, and Ω2 volume (|median relative change| ≥ 10.2%, 48.4%, and 13.7%, respectively) were greater than the corresponding repeatability (CV = 5.19%, 21.3%, and 8.13%, respectively). Significant (p = 0.01) correlation between liver volume-normalized portal venous flow rate and Vb was observed. CONCLUSION: The potential of IVIM to detect physiological (e.g., prandial-induced) changes in microvascular flow in the liver was demonstrated. IVIM data may need to be acquired in a fasting state to avoid confounding prandial effects on IVIM-derived microvascular flow estimates.

articles.title: Learning from the unseen: synthetic data for scoliosis AI segmentation.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Severe scoliosis remains challenging for 3D vertebral segmentation because annotated pathological computed tomography (CT) data are scarce. METHODS: We synthesize scoliosis-like CT volumes by jointly warping public healthy spine scans and labels and then train nnU-Net CNN and PRIMUS models under matched compute. We evaluate on in-house out-of-distribution (OOD) adolescent scoliosis CTs and the public Spine1K dataset. RESULTS: On 18 in-house adolescent scoliosis CTs, the best CNN setting increased mean Dice from 0.765 to 0.842 and vertebra success rate from 73.2 to 81.6%. In 55 surgeon-defined apical labels, mean Dice increased from 0.720 to 0.854. Spine1K performance remained high when synthetic data supplemented real scans; synthetic-only training was less stable. CONCLUSION: Pathology-informed synthetic data improve robustness to severe scoliosis without new annotations or architecture changes. Code and interactive visualizations are available at: https://chepchikvaleri.github.io/synth-data-s/.
